picks.showTitle: James Low - Dzogchen and Buddhist Teachings
picks.title: Emptiness and dzogchen: the song of the cuckoo. [EN-ES] Granada 10.2014
picks.summary:
Teachings by James Low in Granada, Spain, on "Emptiness and Dzogchen," based on Vairocana's text "The Song of the Cuckoo" (31 October - 02 November 2014).

Original audio in English with consecutive Spanish translation by Juan B. García Lázaro.

"Dzogchen is concerned with knowing your own nature. There are many different paths in Buddhism and gradually they became organised into different styles or families. Some are gradual, others less so, but generally it is a matter of knowing what suits you best." ~ James Low

Full audio recordings available at: https://simplybeing.co.uk/audio-recordings
picks.reason: Detailed teachings on emptiness and Dzogchen from a Tibetan Buddhist perspective.

picks.showTitle: Zen Stories & Buddhist Teachings for Sleep by Midnight Monk
picks.title: You Don't Have To Fix Everything… Fall Asleep to Gentle Zen Stories & Buddhist Teachings for Rest
picks.summary: Tonight, we explore the possibility that life does not need to be finished before we are allowed to rest. Through Buddhist wisdom, Zen stories, and gentle reflection, this long-form sleep episode looks at the pressure to improve, resolve, prepare, and become, and what can change when that pressure begins to soften.This is a quiet journey through mindfulness, letting go, self-compassion, acceptance, craving, effort, and the search for inner peace. Rather than asking you to fix your thoughts or reach a particular state, the episode invites a different relationship with whatever is already here:
picks.reason: Gentle Zen stories and teachings on letting go and inner peace for rest.

picks.title: Four Friendly Facts by Kanshin Allison Tait
picks.summary: This Dharma talk explores the Four Noble Truths through Robert Thurman’s playful framing of the “Four Friendly Fun Facts.” Looking at suffering as something to understand rather than escape, the talk considers how self-centeredness creates alienation, how compassion reconnects us with others, and how the Eightfold Path offers a practical way to work with our lives as they actually are. picks.reason: Explores Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path with compassion and impermanence.

picks.title: Enjoy the Dharma! by Kanshin Allison Tait
picks.summary: What does it mean to truly enjoy Zen practice? In this talk, Kanshan explores joy, presence, and the meaning of practicing without a “gaining idea.” Drawing on Suzuki Roshi and Zenkei Blanche Hartman, he reflects on our tendency to think something is missing or wrong with us, and how Zen invites us instead to meet this life with greater openness, balance, love, and joy.------Kanshin Allison Tait - 09/06/26 - Suggested Donation $5
picks.reason: Talk on joy and presence in Zen practice, emphasizing openness and love.

picks.title: Sitting With Your Karma
picks.summary: Given at a One-Day Sitting at the Boulder Zen Center, this talk picks up a question left open in the previous episode, "Sitting Like a Buddha." If zazen is not a means to awakening but its enactment, what about karma? Thoughts, fragments of story, and small triggers of dissatisfaction keep arriving, and we assume awakening means their absence. The talk proposes instead that we are always sitting and living with our karma; what changes is our relationship to it. picks.reason: A talk on sitting with karma and changing our relationship to intentional actions.

picks.title: Buddhist Chanting: Why We Do It | Benefits of Dhamma Recitation | Chant by Heart | Ajahn Dhammasiha
picks.summary: Chanting is an essential part of meditative practice in virtually all Buddhist traditions, and also in other religions. Ajahn Dhammasiha explains the powerful benefits we receive from diligently learning Buddhist chants by heart, from listening to them, and from reciting them regularly. Chanting the teaching of the Buddha develops samatha (tranquility) and samādhi, due to the calming and uplifting effect on our mind. picks.reason: Explains chanting's meditative benefits and its role in Buddhist practice.

picks.title: Appropriate Longing For Buddhists - Domyo
picks.summary: The Buddha's basic teaching is that life is marked by Dukkha, often translated as "suffering", and the cause of that is Tanha, sometimes translated as "craving" or "thirst".  However, in order to practice and maintain our bodhicitta, or way-seeking mind, we actually need to thoughtfully cultivate some desire.  Using the five wisdom energies from Vajrayana teachings as a lens, Domyo describes the five kinds of appropriate longing that can give us insight into our personality type and what we need to nurture in ourselves: red (intimacy), yellow (enjoyment), blue (knowing), green (effectiveness),
picks.reason: Explores appropriate longing in Buddhism using Vajrayana wisdom energies.

picks.title: Don't Neglect Walking Meditation! | Cankama Bhavana | Dhamma Talk | Jongrom | Ajahn Dhammasiha
picks.summary: Walking meditation is in no way inferior to sitting meditation. In fact, for many of us in modern society it can be a more suitable posture than sitting crosslegged (or even full lotus). The way we grow up, always sitting on chairs, we're often not flexible enough for sitting crosslegged. Therefore, walking can help us to continue our meditation for a much longer time. It's also excellent for excercise, and to keep us fit and healthy. picks.reason: Ajahn Dhammasiha explains walking meditation's benefits and practice in daily life.
